Abstract
Appreciating multi-figure paintings requires understanding how
characters relate through subtle cues like gaze alignment, gesture,
and spatial arrangement. We present MIRAGE, an evidence-centric
framework designed to scaffold the exploration of these "micro-
interactions" in multi-figure artworks. While such cues are essential
for deep narrative appreciation, they are often distributed across
complex scenes and difficult for viewers to systematically identify.
Existing vision-language models (VLMs) frequently fail to provide
reliable assistance, offering ungrounded interpretations that lack
traceable visual evidence.
MIRAGE addresses this by constructing a structured intermedi-
ate representation capturing identities, pose cues, and gaze hypothe-
ses. However, the challenge extends beyond extracting these cues

By separating spatial grounding from narrative generation, MI-

relationships through a verifiable evidence layer. We evaluate MI-
RAGE against painting-only VLM baselines using a blind assess-

identity consistency, reduces relational hallucinations, and increases
the coverage of subtle interactions. These findings suggest that
structured grounding can serve as a critical interaction control
layer, providing the necessary scaffolding for a more reliable, trans-
parent, and human-led understanding of complex visual narratives.

1
Introduction
Art appreciation involves complex perceptual and cognitive pro-
cesses shaped by visual organization [18]. In multi-figure paintings,
interpreting the intended narrative often depends on perceiving
micro-interactions: fine-grained relational cues such as gaze align-
ment, gesture contact, body orientation, and spatial proximity that
suggest social intent, emotional tension, and narrative flow. Prior
work demonstrates that humans infer social interactions from such
visual inputs [11, 20, 33], and that these local relational details shape
how viewers understand interpersonal dynamics in art [5, 10]. How-
ever, in complex compositions, these signals are distributed across
many figures and regions of the canvas. Consequently, viewers may
struggle to systematically identify these cues, making it challenging
to move from a broad impression to a grounded reading of how
specific figures relate to one another.
Recent advancements in vision-language models (VLMs) and
AI-assisted art systems demonstrate strong capabilities in holistic
artwork description and conversational exploration [17, 19, 27, 36,
37, 39]. However, these models are rarely architecturally designed
to maintain the fine-grained relational grounding necessary for
micro-interaction analysis. The challenge further extends beyond
detecting such cues to coordinating them during interpretation.
Without an explicit mechanism to organize and reconcile relational
evidence, models often collapse multiple interaction hypotheses
into unstable or weakly grounded interpretations, even when the
underlying signals are correctly identified. When interpreting over-
lapping poses or multiple candidate interactions, VLM outputs fre-
quently drift toward vague narrative summaries, unstable identity
references, and merged attributes [9, 25]. Because these systems
generally operate as opaque models that bypass structured spatial
analysis, they often fail to provide the traceable visual evidence
needed to verify or deepen an interpretive process [3, 31]. This
instability limits their utility for user-centered exploration, par-
ticularly for laymen museum visitors and learners who rely on
understanding who is acting, who is responding, and what visual
evidence supports that reading.
To address this gap, we present MIRAGE, a Micro-Interaction
Relational Architecture for Grounded Exploration in Multi-Figure Art-
works. Positioned as an evidence-centric framework, MIRAGE is
motivated by the premise that the interpretation of complex human
scenes benefits from stabilizing character identities, spatial rela-
tions, and local interaction cues before high-level reasoning occurs.
MIRAGE constructs a structured intermediate representation for
further interpretations. Rather than improving perception alone,
MIRAGE introduces an explicit control layer that stabilizes how
relational evidence is selected, combined, and interpreted. This
representation captures object anchors, pairwise relations, and lo-
calized evidence, effectively separating geometric grounding from
semantic interpretation. By establishing these relations as a foun-
dational layer, MIRAGE allows generated appreciation guidance
to remain tied to identifiable visual evidence rather than relying
solely on global scene impressions.
As an interface framework, MIRAGE facilitates interpretive col-
laboration by exposing subtle figure-to-figure dynamics as inspect-
able evidence. We evaluate MIRAGE by comparing its outputs
against direct image-only prompting of a general-purpose VLM, fo-
cusing on the recovery and interpretability of human-recognizable
micro-interactions. The contributions of this work are:
(1) an evidence-centric architecture that decouples ground-
ing from downstream interpretation, enabling controlled
reasoning over ambiguous multi-figure interactions;
(2) a relationally grounded representation that provides users
with verifiable visual evidence to support the exploration
of subtle character dynamics; and
(3) a systematic evaluation demonstrating that the extra layer
of grounding yields more specific, traceable, and micro-
interaction-aware analysis compared to direct image-only
VLM prompting.
2
Related Work
This research intersects with art appreciation, VLMs, and grounded
scene understanding. We review prior work along five directions:
(1) art appreciation as a relational and interpretive process, (2) LLM
and VLM systems for artwork understanding, (3) grounding and
structured intermediate representations for multimodal reasoning,
(4) micro-interaction in multi-figure artworks, and (5) interactive
dialogue for collaborative art exploration. Together, these threads
underscore the value of a grounding-centered approach to support
the fine-grained interpretation of complex multi-figure scenes.
2.1
Art Appreciation as Relational
Interpretation
Art appreciation involves interpreting how visual elements form
meaningful relationships within a composition. Prior work shows
that artworks are perceived as structured configurations rather
than isolated parts, with meaning emerging through form, spatial
arrangement, and perceptual emphasis [4]. Aesthetic experience

further relies on stages of interpretation and evaluation that build
upon immediate perception [18]. In multi-figure paintings, this pro-
cess is particularly relational, as viewers infer narrative and social
meaning through cues such as gaze, gesture, orientation, and prox-
imity. Prior work on social scene perception indicates that observers
tend to extract interactional structure from visual information [20],
integrating head and body cues to perceive dyadic interaction [33].
Moreover, attention is frequently drawn toward socially interac-
tive regions in naturalistic scenes [28]. Consequently, prior work
suggests that understanding multi-figure artworks depends on per-
ceiving fine-grained visual relations rather than merely identifying
depicted subjects.
2.2
LLMs and VLMs for Artwork Interpretation
Recent advances in LLMs and VLMs facilitate novel forms of compu-
tational support for artwork interpretation, including educational
guidance, formal analysis, question answering, and evaluative di-
alogue. For example, LLaVA-Docent demonstrates how a multi-
modal LLM can support art appreciation education through per-
sonalized conversational tutoring [19]. Concurrently, GalleryGPT
and ArtGPT-4 indicate that art-oriented multimodal models may
produce richer formal analyses and enhance performance on art-
work understanding tasks [6, 37]. Related work exploring artwork
question answering and context-aware cultural heritage chatbots
suggests that integrating external knowledge and contextual de-
scriptions improves responses compared to purely image-based
approaches [9, 25]. Furthermore, systems such as ArtMentor and
recent studies on critique generation suggest that LLMs are increas-
ingly capable of participating in artwork evaluation and interpre-
tive dialogue [3, 39]. However, existing models frequently exhibit
limitations when interpretation relies on contextual accuracy, fine-
grained evidence, or socially embedded reasoning. They commonly
encounter challenges with visual ambiguity, symbolic meaning, and
maintaining consistency across related queries [3, 9, 21]. MIRAGE
extends prior advances in AI-assisted art interpretation by address-
ing these limitations through a grounding-centered architecture,
which systematically separates relational evidence construction
from downstream semantic generation.
2.3
Grounding and Structured Intermediate
Representations
Recent research in vision-language reasoning indicates that explicit
intermediate representations may improve reliability and inter-
pretability by separating perceptual extraction from downstream
inference. In computer vision, scene graph approaches represent
images as entities and relations, providing a stable substrate for
relational reasoning in complex scenes. Foundational works such
as Image Generation from Scene Graphs [16], Neural Motifs [38],
and GQA [15] illustrate how entity-centric representations support
consistent and compositional reasoning.
In parallel, multimodal systems increasingly adopt modular and
interpretable pipelines over purely end-to-end generation. Modern
approaches such as Visual ChatGPT [34] and ViperGPT [30] intro-
duce intermediate stages that decompose perception and reasoning,
aiming to enhance transparency and controllability compared to
opaque one-shot inference. Similarly, Chain-of-Thought prompting
underscores the value of exposing intermediate reasoning steps in
language models [32]. From an HCI perspective, this shift aligns
with the growing emphasis on inspectable AI systems. Guidelines
for Human-AI Interaction [2] suggest that users benefit from under-
standing system behavior and assessing output reliability, motivat-
ing designs that surface structured evidence rather than only final
results. However, prior work largely targets functional tasks such as
visual question answering or navigation, frequently overlooking the
subtle relational cues necessary for art interpretation. In contrast,
visual meaning in artworks heavily relies on compositional rela-
tionships such as gaze, spatial grouping, and tension. Arnheim’s Art
and Visual Perception [4] discusses how such relational structures
shape human interpretation.
Building on these insights, MIRAGE introduces a Grounding Doc-
ument, an inspectable intermediate representation that integrates
character identities, spatial anchors, and localized relational evi-
dence prior to semantic interpretation. By formulating grounding as
a queryable layer, MIRAGE bridges structured scene representation,
modular multimodal reasoning, and human-centered interpretabil-
ity to facilitate the exploration of complex multi-figure artworks.
2.4
Micro-Interaction in Multi-Figure Artworks
We define micro-interactions as localized, fine-grained relational
configurations between figures, or between figures and salient ob-
jects, that shape scene interpretation. These interactions emerge
from subtle visual cues—such as gaze, gesture, posture, and proximity—
that are extensively studied as social signals in human percep-
tion [24]. Because observers naturally integrate multiple weak sig-
nals to infer interpersonal dynamics [1], relational meaning rarely
stems from a single isolated cue. For example, while gaze is critical
for coordinating shared attention [14, 29], it must be contextually
combined with other spatial signals to convey complex narratives
like support or tension.
Despite their importance, current computational approaches to
art understanding heavily prioritize global captioning. By over-
looking localized relational structures, fine-grained interactions
are frequently omitted, inconsistently described, or hallucinated
during downstream interpretation. MIRAGE addresses this limita-
tion by formalizing micro-interactions as structured, inspectable
units grounded in verifiable visual evidence. Through the explicit
representation of stable character identities, spatial anchors, and
cue-level signals, the framework provides the necessary scaffolding
for users to systematically reason about subtle relationships that
holistic descriptions otherwise obscure.
2.5
Interactive Dialogue for Art Exploration
Conversational systems support interactive sensemaking by en-
abling users to iteratively probe system outputs, explore multi-
ple perspectives, and incrementally construct meaning [2, 22, 23].
This dynamic exploration is particularly crucial for art interpreta-
tion, where understanding emerges over time rather than through
single-pass observation. However, many existing systems rely on
free-form generation without explicit visual grounding. Because
effective human-AI interaction requires transparency and reliability
to build trust [2], ungrounded conversational agents often fail to

ensure interpretations remain consistent, verifiable, and strictly
tied to specific visual details in complex multi-figure scenes.
MIRAGE extends this prior work by anchoring conversational
dialogue within a queryable evidence layer that incorporates stable
character identities, object anchors, and relation-level cues. Rather
than treating dialogue as a strictly generative process, this approach
assists users in iteratively exploring artworks while maintaining an
inspectable connection between high-level semantic interpretations
and localized visual evidence.
3
System Architecture
MIRAGE supports micro-interaction understanding in multi-figure
paintings by introducing a structured grounding representation
prior to interpretation. Instead of relying on end-to-end captioning,
MIRAGE decomposes a painting into character anchors with stable
identities, objects that organize interaction, geometric interaction
cues, and pairwise relation states, which are consolidated into a
grounding document for downstream reasoning. This design en-
ables interpretation over explicit, inspectable interaction structure
rather than implicit inference from the raw image.
3.1
Face-First Character Detection & Object
Anchoring
MIRAGE initializes a structured grounding space by identifying
both character and object anchors. Rather than relying on body-
first detection, we adopt a face-first strategy in which faces serve as
stable identity seeds and are later expanded to body-level regions.
This design prioritizes identity stability in paintings, where full-
body cues are often unreliable due to stylization, occlusion, and
non-photographic poses.

3.2
Character-Centric Grounding Construction

figure into a structured character profile,

The reliability of these geometric cues depends on grounding
availability. As shown in Figure 2, when both face and body re-
gions are detected, MIRAGE recovers a full skeleton and produces
usable pose and gaze estimates. When body support is missing,
pose inference is disabled to avoid introducing unsupported geo-
metric signals. This conditional use of geometry ensures that only
grounded structural evidence is propagated to later stages.
To resolve ambiguity in geometric hypotheses, MIRAGE per-
forms VLM-based semantic enrichment using GPT-5.4. Each char-
acter is described under a stable ID using both local crops and the
full image, focusing on interaction-relevant attributes like body lan-
guage, facial expression, object interaction, and attention direction.
Geometry provides candidate interaction structure, while the VLM
refines and disambiguates these signals under visual context.
Finally, MIRAGE extracts scene-level context (e.g., composition
and setting) to support the interpretation of local interactions. To-
gether, character profiles, geometric cues, and VLM enrichment
produce interaction-ready character states that serve as the basis
for subsequent relational grounding.

3.3
Relational Grounding
Given interaction-ready character states, MIRAGE constructs pair-
wise relation records for all character pairs. Instead of directly
producing free-form descriptions, relations are first represented as
structured evidence derived from spatial and geometric cues.
For each pair (𝑖, 𝑗), MIRAGE records normalized inter-character
distance, bounding-box overlap (IoU), relative position, and size
ratio. These quantitative metrics are combined with candidate inter-
action cues derived from pose direction vectors, proximity thresh-
olds, and shared object references. A localized pair crop, defined by
the union of the two character bounding boxes with a 15% spatial
margin, is extracted to preserve relation-specific visual context.
This process yields relation states encoding interaction-aware
structures. Unlike single-character representations, these states
capture the foundational micro-interactions emerging from rela-
tive configurations. By storing each relation as a structured record,
MIRAGE establishes a relational reference for downstream lan-
guage generation, serving as a set of algorithmically derived anchor
points. Unlike conventional conversational agents that rely solely
on unconstrained generation [31, 39], this structural representa-
tion mitigates the premature collapse of foundational evidence into
vague natural-language summaries, ensuring that the subsequent
generative process builds upon localized, inspectable signals.
3.4
Grounding Document Assembly
MIRAGE consolidates the extracted scene-level, character-level,
and relation-level evidence into a unified grounding document
formatted in Markdown. It serves as a structured intermediate
representation, organizing heterogeneous pipeline signals into a
single, coherent reference baseline for downstream reasoning.
The Markdown schema integrates three primary domains into a
continuous textual structure. Scene Context encodes global compo-
sition and semantic tags. Character Profiles store stable identifiers
(e.g., C1, C2), spatial attributes, and pose-derived signals. Concur-
rently, Pairwise Relations capture localized interaction evidence
alongside shared object anchors.
The selection of Markdown as the structural interface is based
on recent empirical findings regarding LLM performance. Stud-
ies indicate that macro-formatting significantly influences LLM
comprehension, with well-structured formats like Markdown im-
proving reasoning accuracy in complex text processing tasks [7, 13].
Furthermore, LLMs exhibit notable sensitivity to spurious features
and arbitrary formatting variations [26]. By standardizing heteroge-
neous visual signals into a predictable Markdown schema, MIRAGE
mitigates formatting-induced performance fluctuations, making
geometric data more accessible and stable for VLM processing.
This grounding document acts as the primary interface between
visual analysis and generative interpretation. By treating algorith-
mic signals as a foundational reference, the document allows the
VLM to anchor its open-ended semantic interpretations and artis-
tic reasoning to geometric constraints. This structured approach
reduces the likelihood of errors associated with inferring complex,
multi-figure geometries directly from raw pixels.
Geometry–VLM Integration and Conflict Preservation. MIRAGE
uses a geometry-first design with VLM refinement. Geometry pro-
vides spatial structure, while VLMs resolve higher-level cues such
as gaze and intent that are ambiguous from 2D information alone.
When disagree, MIRAGE preserves both interpretations instead of
forcing a single decision. This allows the system to expose uncer-
tainty and support reasoning over multiple possible interactions.
3.5
Grounded VLM Interpretation
In the final architectural stage, MIRAGE employs a Vision-Language
Model (GPT-5.4) as its grounded interpretation engine. Building
upon the structural interface established in the previous stage,
the generation process shifts away from analyzing raw pixels in
isolation—a method inherently prone to identity blending and spa-
tial hallucination in stylized, multi-figure compositions. Instead, the

VLM executes its interpretive reasoning directly over the assembled
Markdown grounding document. This document defines a struc-
tured reasoning space in which identities, relations, and evidential
constraints are explicitly encoded, limiting the model’s inference
to grounded interaction hypotheses.
This generative phase is guided by targeted system prompts that
enforce constrained extrapolation over the structured grounding
representation. The model is instructed to treat the provided schema
as an immutable reference baseline. Operating strictly within these
algorithmic boundaries, the VLM engages in abductive reasoning
to articulate implicit emotional dynamics, interpret subtle visual
nuances omitted by pose estimators, and synthesize broader art
historical contexts. This establishes an explicit control layer over
how relational evidence is selected, combined, and interpreted dur-
ing generation. The primary constraint requires that higher-order
narrative inferences logically align with the derived spatial and
semantic anchors, effectively preventing the invention of unsup-
ported relational dynamics.
When processing the intentional modality conflicts preserved
within the document, the system prompts the VLM to evaluate
these algorithmic disagreements as explicit indicators of visual am-
biguity. Rather than attempting a deterministic override, the model
conceptually integrates these discrepancies, recognizing them as
potential artifacts of complex occlusions, stylized drapery, or delib-
erate compositional tension inherent to the artwork.
Ultimately, this reasoning mechanism yields nuanced, evidence-
based scene narratives and pairwise interaction analyses. While
this scaffolded approach significantly enhances structural fidelity,
the system’s overall reliability naturally remains bounded by the
performance characteristics of the underlying detection and pose
estimation pipelines.
4
System Capabilities
MIRAGE provides a structured representation of multi-character
scenes by systematically organizing visual evidence—such as char-
acter identity, pose, gaze, spatial relations, and object-mediated
interactions—into distinct relational components. The system builds
an interpretable framework for interaction analysis. To illustrate
these capabilities, we present a qualitative comparison between
a baseline VLM and the MIRAGE-augmented model across sev-
eral representative artwork scenarios, detailed in Figure 4. The
following sections explore how this structured grounding enhances
interaction understanding across four conceptual levels: recover-
ing fine-grained micro-interactions at the local level, modeling
object-mediated connections at the intermediate level, preserving
multimodal ambiguity at the representation level, and surfacing
directional organization at the global level.
4.1
Local: Fine-Grained Relations
Standard VLMs often produce global summaries that lack structural
representation of interactions between specific characters. MIRAGE
addresses this limitation by constructing a grounding layer that en-
codes localized interaction cues derived from spatial and relational
evidence, enabling stable and verifiable reasoning.
Deconstructing Composite Agents in High Overlap. In The Birth
of Venus, the airborne figures (C1, C2) exhibit substantial spatial
overlap (IoU = 0.542), posing a challenge for maintaining distinct
character identities. While a baseline GPT-5.4 provides a metaphor-
ical interpretation describing them as “fused in movement”, the
MIRAGE-augmented model instead represents them as two distinct
entities with strong spatial coupling. By leveraging this quantitative
IoU data, the model captures their coordinated configuration and
maintains a structured representation of their interaction.
Subtle Contact Recognition. In Et in Arcadia ego (Fig. 4, Row 2),
MIRAGE identifies a localized interaction where C4 places a hand
on C3’s back, supported by spatial overlap (IoU = 0.140). This is
encoded as a discrete relation grounded in physical contact.
4.2
Intermediate: Object Anchoring
Interactions in multi-figure artworks are often organized around
shared objects and focal points. MIRAGE models these structures
by structurally linking characters through object anchors, which
enables the representation of object-mediated interactions rather
than treating characters as isolated entities.
Triangulated Attention via Anchors. In Et in Arcadia ego, MI-
RAGE constructs a relation structure where C2 and C3’s “pointing”
gestures are both linked to the tomb_inscription in the center of
the image (vlm_obj_002). By identifying this shared reference, the
system treats the tomb as a central interaction anchor, organizing
multiple character actions into a coherent relational topology rather
than evaluating them as independent poses.
Object-Mediated Interaction. In The Birth of Venus, the interaction
between the two characters on the left is mediated by the embrac-
ing_drapery (vlm_obj_004). MIRAGE encodes this as a shared object-
linked relation, where the artifact provides a structural connection
between the figures, allowing the model to distinguish intentional
object-mediated interaction from incidental spatial proximity.
4.3
Representation: Conflict Awareness
Rather than collapsing visual ambiguity into a single deterministic
label, MIRAGE is designed to preserve conflicting signals that arise
between the geometric pose estimation (YOLOv8x-pose) and the
semantic enrichment (GPT-5.4) stages. This conflict preservation
enables the system to retain multiple interpretations derived from
different modalities, supporting transparent and evidence-aware
reasoning.
Semantic vs. Geometric Dissonance. In Et in Arcadia ego (Fig. 4,
Row 3), the VLM describes C2 as “kneeling” (semantic), whereas
the pose estimation module infers a “standing/crouching” posture
based on geometric cues. This discrepancy illustrates the potential
divergence between high-level semantic interpretation and low-
level spatial estimation.
Uncertainty-Aware Representation. Instead of forcing consensus,
MIRAGE retains both interpretations under a Conflict Preserved
status. This approach allows downstream reasoning to operate over
multiple hypotheses rather than relying on a single resolved label.

“stable kneeling position,” while the MIRAGE-enabled model incor-
porates the posture discrepancy into its interpretation, reflecting

4.4
Global: Scene Topology
Beyond isolated pairwise relations, MIRAGE captures higher-level
interaction structures across the scene. By combining local rela-
tional signals, the system forms a global interaction topology that
reflects how characters are spatially and directionally organized.
Directional Interaction Structure. The system identifies asym-
metric configurations where multiple relational cues (e.g., gaze
direction, pose orientation, spatial arrangement) converge toward
a central figure, such as C3 in The Birth of Venus. This conver-
gence forms a structured pattern of directional relations, indicating
that characters participate in scene-level organization rather than
merely connecting locally.
Role-Like Structural Differentiation. The grounded representa-
tion enables the differentiation of characters based on their rela-
tional patterns. For example, some characters primarily contribute
outgoing directional cues (e.g., gaze or motion toward others),
while others serve as focal recipients or participate through object-
mediated interactions (e.g., C4 in the Venus scene). This differentia-
tion emerges organically from the relational structure rather than
relying on pre-defined categorical labels.
Across the presented examples, MIRAGE shifts interaction under-
standing from implicit description to structured, evidence-based rea-
soning. At the local level, it recovers fine-grained micro-interactions
utilizing localized spatial relations. At the intermediate level, it
links characters through shared anchors, enabling the representa-
tion of object-mediated interactions. At the representation level, it
preserves ambiguity across modalities, supporting conflict-aware
reasoning without forcing premature resolution. At the global level,
it organizes relational signals into coherent interaction structures.
These capabilities address key challenges in multi-figure interaction
understanding, particularly identity stability, relational ambiguity,
and the representation of grounded interaction structures.

Evaluation
We evaluate MIRAGE through a two-part protocol examining out-
put quality and user interaction. Section 5.1 quantitatively compares

reasoning, transparency, and human-AI collaboration.
5.1
Quantitative Evaluation
We design our evaluation to directly measure the core challenges
identified in multi-figure interaction understanding. Specifically,
we assess (1) identity stability to address character-level drift, (2)
interaction accuracy to evaluate the detection of meaningful rela-
tions, (3) directional reasoning to capture interaction structure and
flow, and (4) grounding-aware reasoning to ensure interpretations
are supported by explicit visual evidence.
5.1.1
Dataset & Protocol. We evaluate whether structured ground-
ing improves micro-interaction understanding in multi-figure art-
works compared to non-grounded baselines. While VLMs often
identify isolated perceptual cues, understanding micro-interactions
requires integrating relational signals (e.g., gaze, posture, spatial
configuration) into coherent interpretations. We designed a con-
trolled evaluation protocol to measure identity consistency, inter-
action correctness, directional reasoning, and evidence usage.
Our dataset comprises 15 multi-figure images spanning three
categories to ensure structural variety: 5 canonical paintings, 5
lesser-known artworks (to mitigate memorization bias), and 5 gen-

selected 5 to 7 key interaction instances per image, encompass-

To establish a ground truth, we constructed a reference set based

into visually grounded states like support, guidance, or shared at-

Annotations were strictly bound to observable cues such as gaze
alignment, physical contact, or spatial proximity. Disagreements
among annotators were resolved through consensus discussion.

conditions are evaluated under identical question templates and

MIRAGE: A Micro-Interaction Relational Architecture for Grounded Exploration in Multi-Figure Artworks
5.2
User Study
To complement the quantitative evaluation in Section 5.1, we con-
ducted a user study (N = 8) to explore how MIRAGE might influence
users’ interpretive process, focusing on evidence-based reasoning,
transparency, and human-AI collaboration. Participants interpreted
a multi-figure painting in two phases: independent observation
and MIRAGE-assisted analysis using the image, relation visual-
ization, and grounding document with a GPT-5.4 assistant. They
completed three tasks—identifying micro-interactions, determining
the attention center, and resolving ambiguity—and were addition-
ally allowed open-ended questioning. Participants then completed
a questionnaire measuring self-reported interpretive confidence,
grounding, transparency, collaboration, and cognitive load.
5.2.1
Study Design and Questionnaire Analysis.
Questionnaire Design. To evaluate the utility of MIRAGE’s decou-
pled perception and interpretation pipeline, we administered a post-
task questionnaire designed to capture subjective user feedback
across four core dimensions. To assess the cognitive friction some-
times associated with standard VLMs, we adapted core dimensions
from the Raw NASA-TLX [12]—specifically mental demand, tem-
poral demand, performance, effort, and frustration. These metrics
were contextualized to estimate the cognitive workload involved
in aligning system-generated interpretations with visual evidence.
To better reflect the specific goals of the MIRAGE framework, we
augmented the survey with three custom dimensions. First, In-
terpretive Understanding assessed users’ self-reported ability to
comprehend relational dynamics, identify subtle micro-interactions,
and construct coherent narratives. Second, Visual Groundedness
and Stability explored the system’s capacity to reduce ungrounded
interpretations by measuring users’ perceived ease of verifying
claims against localized visual evidence and tracking character
identities. Third, Human-AI Collaboration examined how the rea-
soning transparency of intermediate structured data supported
system trust and a sense of collaborative agency, as opposed to
passive consumption. All custom items were rated on a 7-point
Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). The adapted
cognitive load items were anchored on a 7-point scale ranging from
very low to very high, with the performance item reverse-scaled.
Results. Participants reported generally positive ratings for in-
terpretive understanding. Relational comprehension (Q1: M = 5.00,
SD = 1.69) and narrative construction (Q3: M = 5.75, SD = 1.04)
were above the midpoint, while micro-interaction discovery (Q2:
M = 6.13, SD = 0.99) was rated particularly high, indicating that
MIRAGE helped users notice subtle visual cues.
Measures of visual groundedness were also strongly rated. Par-
ticipants indicated that system interpretations were clearly linked
to localized visual evidence (Q4: M = 5.88, SD = 0.99) and could
be verified with minimal effort (Q5: M = 5.63, SD = 1.30). Identity
consistency (Q6: M = 5.38, SD = 1.69) was similarly rated positively,
suggesting stable tracking of characters across interactions.
In terms of human–AI collaboration, participants reported mod-
erate to high levels of trust (Q7: M = 4.50, SD = 1.20), while ratings
for reasoning transparency (Q8: M = 5.25, SD = 1.49) and collab-
orative agency (Q9: M = 5.63, SD = 1.19) were consistently above
the midpoint. This suggests that users perceived the interaction
as a cooperative interpretive process supported by the system’s
structured representation.
Despite the additional information provided by MIRAGE, cogni-
tive workload remained low. Mental effort (Q10: M = 3.00, SD = 1.07)
was centered around the lower-mid range, and frustration levels
(Q11: M = 2.13, SD = 0.99) were consistently low. This suggests that
MIRAGE enhances interpretive capability while maintaining low
cognitive overhead.
5.2.2
Shifts Toward Evidence-Based Interpretation. A significant
shift occurred from the "narrative-heavy" descriptions typical of
the independent phase toward evidence-anchored reasoning. Partici-
pants moved beyond subjective tropes, instead adopting MIRAGE’s
relational vocabulary—such as gaze vectors, physical contact, and
spatial proximity (e.g., R5, C1—C4)—to justify their claims in a more
explicit and structured manner. This transition suggests the ground-
ing document functions as a cognitive scaffold, prompting users to
reconcile high-level intuition with low-level visual primitives and
supporting a more structured mode of perception.
5.2.3
Collaborative Negotiation of Evidence. Rather than treating
MIRAGE as an authoritative oracle, participants engaged in a pro-
cess of evidence negotiation. When questioning system outputs (e.g.,
gaze relationships), users utilized the provided geometric justifica-
tions to refine their own hypotheses. This interaction pattern indi-
cates that MIRAGE facilitates a collaborative interpretive process
where user intuition and structured evidence are jointly considered,
preserving human agency throughout the analysis.
5.2.4
Navigating Ambiguity as an Interpretive Resource. MIRAGE
prioritizes grounded evidence, maintaining analytical rigor even
when user hypotheses conflict with pose-derived skeletal data or
relational estimates. Crucially, the externalization of system un-
certainty (e.g., conflicting gaze or posture cues) functioned as an
interpretive prompt rather than a technical failure. Users leveraged
this transparency to explore nuanced sub-narratives, transforming
visual ambiguity from a limitation into a resource for reflective
reasoning and deeper engagement with the artwork.
5.2.5
User-Driven Exploration and Reflective Agency. During open-
ended interactions, participants transitioned from passive obser-
vation to active reflection, using MIRAGE to iteratively test self-
directed hypotheses. By comparing their evolving interpretations
with the grounding evidence, users expanded their perspectives
toward alternative focal points. However, this scaffolding also re-
vealed a critical trade-off: while structured guidance promotes rigor,
it may introduce interpretive bias by bounding the scope of per-
ception to system-generated hypotheses, highlighting an area for
future balance between guidance and autonomy.
6
Discussion
While the quantitative and qualitative evaluations suggest that the
MIRAGE architecture enhances the structural fidelity and evidence-
based grounding of multi-figure artwork interpretation, the frame-
work’s broader contribution lies in its alternative interaction para-
digm. The system aims to shift the locus of interpretation from the
opaque latent space of a vision-language model back to the user,
mediated by an inspectable evidence layer. This section articulates


Chiu et al.
the potential design implications of this approach for human-AI
co-reasoning, critically examines the current technical boundaries
of the system, and outlines a roadmap for future deployment.
6.1
Implications for Human-AI Co-Reasoning
Current VLM interaction paradigms often treat systems as author-
itative oracles, producing seamless end-to-end narratives. Obser-
vations from the MIRAGE evaluation suggest that disrupting this
seamlessness through structured intermediate representations can
substantially influence how users engage with visual content. By
prompting the system to externalize its perceptual primitives—such
as spatial overlap, gaze vectors, and object anchors—the interface
provides a scaffold for the user’s interpretive process. Participants
frequently moved away from relying on generic narrative tropes
and instead tended to adopt the system’s structural vocabulary to
ground their interpretive claims. This indicates that intermediate
representations do more than augment output; they serve as cogni-
tive scaffolds that anchor high-level intuition in verifiable, low-level
visual evidence.
Furthermore, the intentional exposure of system ambiguity and
modality conflicts appeared to serve as a valuable mechanism for
preserving human agency. When the system surfaced discrepancies
between geometric pose estimation and semantic inference, partici-
pants generally did not interpret this merely as a technical failure.
Instead, they often utilized the exposed uncertainty as an invitation
to negotiate the interpretation, treating the AI as a collaborative
sounding board instead of a definitive truth-teller. This finding
aligns with the HCI concept of seamful design [8], suggesting that
in highly subjective domains like art appreciation, rendering the
AI’s internal conflicts visible can be more productive than enforc-
ing premature algorithmic consensus. It helps foster a space for
transparent co-reasoning where users may feel more equipped to
question, refine, and override system hypotheses.
However, this scaffolding highlights a notable trade-off between
structural interpretability and perceptual bias. While the visualiza-
tion of directional cues and relational anchors helped ground user
reasoning, participants noted that these visual artifacts could simul-
taneously direct or constrain their interpretive focus. By drawing
attention to system-generated hypotheses, the interface may intro-
duce an anchoring bias, potentially limiting the user’s capacity for
open-ended, divergent perception. In symbolic or highly ambiguous
contexts, over-structuring the visual field might inadvertently fore-
close alternative narratives that fall outside the system’s geometric
vocabulary. Navigating this tension between necessary evidentiary
guidance and the preservation of unstructured human intuition
remains a central challenge for the design of future generative
interfaces in creative domains.
6.2
Limitations
While MIRAGE provides a structured representational layer, its
efficacy is constrained by its foundational perception and spatial
mapping modules. Because YOLOv8 is primarily trained on photo-
graphic images, the resulting domain shift degrades detection in
stylized, non-Western, abstract, or heavily occluded compositions.
Furthermore, relying on 2D spatial metrics to infer interactions is
inherently limited; in artworks utilizing hierarchical proportion or
compressed depth, 2D proximity does not reliably indicate a nar-
rative or physical connection. This can yield misleading relational
anchors despite VLM contextualization. Future work could address
these visual processing limits through domain-adaptive fine-tuning,
contour-based extraction, or monocular depth estimation.
Additionally, the system remains subject to the probabilistic
nature of generative models. While the grounding document effec-
tively mitigates semantic hallucinations, it cannot entirely elimi-
nate them or prevent the misinterpretation of ambiguous gestures.
Moreover, the architectural choice to preserve modality conflicts
assumes the downstream VLM possesses robust conflict-resolution
capabilities. Future research should investigate neuro-symbolic rea-
soning or knowledge-graph integration to more firmly anchor these
generative interpretations in verifiable art-historical contexts.
6.3
Future Work
While our evaluation demonstrates system-centric improvements
on a curated dataset, validating MIRAGE within broader HCI con-
texts requires longitudinal studies with art historians, students,
and museum visitors. These studies will assess changes in interpre-
tive confidence, the identification of subtle micro-interactions, and
the usability of the grounding document across a wider variety of
artistic movements, solidifying structured grounding as a robust
paradigm for computational art appreciation.
Beyond analytical interpretation, MIRAGE can be extended to
support multi-perspective narrative generation. By conditioning
first-person, character-driven narratives on the grounding document—
specifically integrating relational cues like gaze and spatial alignment—
the system can generate evidence-consistent interpretations. Inves-
tigating whether multiple character-centered narratives enhance
user reasoning around relational ambiguity will further establish
MIRAGE as a dynamic narrative interface.
Finally, the architecture’s decoupled nature facilitates physical
museum deployment via edge computing. Processing geometric
grounding offline into lightweight Markdown allows live interac-
tions to be driven by smaller, locally hosted language models. This
localized deployment minimizes latency, guarantees visitor privacy,
and empowers institutions to enforce operational guardrails. The
primary technical challenge for this deployment will be determin-
ing if lightweight models possess the requisite abductive reasoning
to reliably interpret structural constraints and modality conflicts
without increasing semantic hallucination.
7
Conclusion
This work presented MIRAGE, a computational architecture de-
signed to support multi-figure artwork interpretation by stabilizing
relational reasoning. By separating geometric scene grounding
from high-level semantic generation, the system constructs an in-
termediate representation that links character identities, object
anchors, and spatial configurations. This approach shifts the ana-
lytical process from relying solely on end-to-end implicit inference
to reasoning over a structured, inspectable set of visual evidence.
Our quantitative evaluation shows that anchoring VLMs with
a dedicated grounding document improves character consistency
and reduces hallucinated relational claims. Furthermore, the sys-
tem’s design choice preserving discrepancies between semantic


MIRAGE: A Micro-Interaction Relational Architecture for Grounded Exploration in Multi-Figure Artworks
inferences and spatial estimates offers a more transparent method
for handling visual ambiguity. Instead of forcing resolution, these
conflicts allow downstream models to incorporate multiple hy-
potheses, reflecting the inherent complexity of interpreting stylized
or densely populated compositions.
Ultimately, MIRAGE serves as a step toward more reliable human-
AI collaboration in visual art analysis. By introducing an explicit
intermediate representation, the system shifts interpretation from
implicit generation to controlled reasoning over structured visual
evidence. While the current evaluation highlights improvements
in system-centric micro-interaction recovery, the broader value of
this architecture lies in its potential to facilitate interactive and
evidence-based exploration. Future integration of this framework
into user-facing applications will help determine how structured
relational scaffolds influence human interpretive confidence and
collaborative discovery in art appreciation.

Questionnaire
The post-study questionnaire consisted of 16 Likert-scale items
and one open-ended question. Items were grouped into four di-
mensions: (1) interpretive confidence and appreciation, (2) visual
groundedness and stability, (3) trust and human–AI collaboration,
and (4) cognitive load and frustration.
These dimensions were designed to capture key aspects of MI-
RAGE, including micro-interaction discovery, evidence-based rea-
soning, and interaction transparency.
All Likert-scale items were rated on a 7-point scale unless other-
wise noted. For agreement-based items, 1 indicates strongly disagree
and 7 indicates strongly agree. For cognitive load items, 1 indicates
very low and 7 indicates very high. The performance item is reverse-
scaled (1 = perfect, 7 = failure). Cognitive load items were adapted
from the NASA-TLX framework.
Participants completed the questionnaire immediately after fin-
ishing the MIRAGE-assisted interpretation phase. All items were
answered based on their experience interacting with the system,
including the grounding document, relation visualization, and con-
versational assistant.
Participants were instructed to reflect on both their interpretive
process and their interaction with the system when responding to
the questions.

Example Prompt
The following system prompt is used during the MIRAGE-assisted
interaction phase. It constrains the language model to perform
structured, evidence-based reasoning grounded in the MIRAGE
representation, rather than generating unconstrained descriptions.
You are an assistant for interpreting multi-figure paintings
using MIRAGE grounding materials.
Inputs:
(1) the original image,
(2) a MIRAGE grounding document, and
(3) a relation visualization.
Objective:
Support evidence-based interpretation of micro-interactions
between characters.
Grounding Rules:
1. Treat MIRAGE as the primary evidence layer.
• Prioritize resolved gaze and posture.
• Use relation records (R*) and object anchors (O*) as
primary references.
• Treat geometry and intermediate outputs as supporting
or conflicting evidence.
2. Base all claims on grounded visual evidence.
• Use gaze, posture, gesture, touch, proximity,
overlap, and object-centered attention.
• Do NOT introduce information not supported by the
grounding document or image.
3. Handle ambiguity explicitly.
• If multiple interpretations are plausible, state
them.
• If evidence conflicts, describe the conflict instead
of resolving it silently.
4. Use structured references.
• Refer to characters as C1, C2, ...
• Refer to relations as R0, R1, ...
• Refer to objects as O1, O2, ...
5. Limit unsupported inference.
• Do not invent intentions or narratives beyond
available evidence.
• If evidence is weak or insufficient, state the
uncertainty.
6. Contextual knowledge.
• General art knowledge may be used only to support or
interpret grounded evidence,not to replace it.
Response Format:
(1) Claim
(2) Supporting evidence (with explicit references to C*,
R*, O*)
(3) Optional contextual interpretation (if relevant)
(4) Uncertainty or ambiguity (if any)
Interaction Protocol:
Treat the user’s input as a hypothesis.
• Align with supported components.
• Refine unclear elements.
• Explain conflicts without rejecting the hypothesis.
• Maintain a collaborative, evidence-driven
interpretation process.

User:
Is C1 directly touching C2?
Assistant:

2. Supporting evidence
• C1 grips O1 (inner_tube), not C2 directly
• C2’s body is supported via O1
• Proximity between C1’s hands and C2’s leg is high,
but no verified overlap
3. Optional interpretation
This suggests object-mediated support rather than direct
physical interaction.
4. Uncertainty
The proximity may visually suggest contact, but grounding
does not confirm it.
Abstract: Appreciating multi-figure paintings requires understanding how characters relate through subtle cues like gaze alignment, gesture, and spatial arrangement. We present MIRAGE, an evidence-centric framework designed to scaffold the exploration of these "micro- interactions" in multi-figure artworks. While such cues are essential for deep narrative appreciation, they are often distributed across complex scenes and difficult for viewers to systematically identify. Existing vision-language models (VLMs) frequently fail to provide reliable assistance, offering ungrounded interpretations that lack traceable visual evidence. MIRAGE addresses this by constructing a structured intermedi- ate representation capturing identities, pose cues, and gaze hypothe- ses. However, the challenge extends beyond extracting these cues arXiv:2604.23788v1 [cs.CV] 26 Apr 2026 Chiu et al. to coordinating them during interpretation. Without an explicit mechanism to organize and reconcile relational evidence, models often collapse multiple interaction hypotheses into a single unsta- ble or weakly grounded narrative, even when low-level signals are available. This representation allows users to verify how high-level interpretations are anchored in low-level visual facts. By separating spatial grounding from narrative generation, MI- RAGE enables users to inspect and reason about figure-to-figure relationships through a verifiable evidence layer. We evaluate MI- RAGE against painting-only VLM baselines using a blind assess- ment protocol. Results show that MIRAGE significantly improves identity consistency, reduces relational hallucinations, and increases the coverage of subtle interactions. These findings suggest that structured grounding can serve as a critical interaction control layer, providing the necessary scaffolding for a more reliable, trans- parent, and human-led understanding of complex visual narratives.
